reason: The myoblasts must fuse into a multinucleated muscle fibre, and the fusion proteins are positioned at their adjoining membranes.
expectation: The myoblasts will fuse into a long muscle fibre with multiple nuclei.

effect: The fused fibre has sliding filaments ready, but actin’s grip sites remain covered; the calcium signal is the likely next step.
reaction: The distinction between one fibre and its many nuclei is useful.
reason: A calcium pulse around the filaments should enable the fibre to contract.
expectation: Calcium will expose actin’s binding sites so the filaments can produce a pull.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites and enabled filament sliding; the fibre now needs calcium removed to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between filaments sliding and shortening is clear.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes should return calcium to storage and allow the fibre to relax.
expectation: ATP-powered pumps will reduce calcium around the filaments, allowing the fibre to relax and be ready for another signal.

effect: Calcium pumping stopped the pull and completed the fibre goal; the next task is to assemble and attach both muscles.
reaction: It is useful that relaxation requires ATP and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces that the relaxed fibres can fill.
expectation: The fibres will be arranged within the biceps sheaths and connected to their tendons.

effect: The fibres first needed collagen-rich connective layers to form fascicles; there are enough bundles for both muscles.
reaction: The intermediate bundling step makes the sheath connection clearer.
reason: The fascicles can now fill the biceps muscle-head spaces and connect to its tendons.
expectation: The fascicles will form a biceps within its sheaths, continuous with the tendons.

effect: The fascicles formed the biceps, with connective tissue transferring force to its tendons.
reaction: The force-transfer inset makes the tendon connection clearer.
reason: The remaining fascicles should fill the triceps sheaths in the same way.
expectation: The fascicles will form a triceps with tendons extending toward its attachments.

effect: Both muscles are assembled; their tendons still need attachment to the arm skeleton.
reaction: The three triceps heads have distinct origins, which makes their arrangement clearer.
reason: The biceps tendons run toward the shoulder and radius, so the movable skeleton is the natural attachment partner.
expectation: The biceps will attach across the elbow to the arm skeleton.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attachment across the elbow.

effect: The biceps is attached and flexes the elbow; the assembly still needs an extensor.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps’ pull on the radius clear.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle and fits the extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach across the elbow and extend it by pulling on the ulna.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm assembly; its posterior attachment turns a pull into elbow extension.
reaction: The contrasting tendon positions make the opposing movements clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: The calcium-driven contraction and ATP-powered return to relaxation were most worthwhile: the planned sequences distinguish filament sliding from filament shortening and show why relaxation also needs energy.

leastWorthwhile.text: Filling the two muscle sheaths was somewhat repetitive, although the distinct heads and tendon routes added anatomical context.

surprise.text: The fibre lengthens under an outside pull after calcium is pumped back into storage; relaxation is not presented as the fibre actively pushing itself longer.

arbitrary.text: I initially tried putting the fibre directly into the biceps sheaths; the required fascicle-building step was not obvious beforehand. The compatibility feedback and resulting connective-layer description explained it afterward.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the constructions connected cellular machinery to whole-arm movement, though the planned pictures and concise prose alone cannot establish student comprehension.
